docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: This document defines how Clean Architecture is applied within the backend services of Halal-Queue. It ensures separation of concerns, high testability, and independence from frameworks and external services.

docs.title: Layers
docs.text:
The architecture consists of four primary layers, with dependencies strictly pointing inward toward the Domain.

Presentation Layer (Controllers/Resolvers)
       │
       ▼
Application Layer (Use Cases/CQRS)
       │
       ▼
Domain Layer (Entities/Value Objects/Interfaces)
       ▲
       │
Infrastructure Layer (Database/External APIs)

docs.title: 1. Domain Layer (The Core)
docs.text: The Domain Layer holds the absolute truth of the business logic. - Contains: Entities, Value Objects, Domain Events, and Repository Interfaces (Ports). - Dependencies: None. It must not import from any other layer or framework (except core language features).

docs.title: 2. Application Layer
docs.text: Orchestrates the business use cases and translates external requests into domain operations. - Contains: Use Cases (Services), CQRS Commands/Queries, Command Handlers, and DTOs. - Dependencies: Depends ONLY on the Domain layer. It interacts with the outside world strictly through the interfaces (Ports) defined in the Domain.

docs.title: 3. Presentation Layer
docs.text: Responsible for delivering information over the network and parsing incoming requests. - Contains: REST Controllers, GraphQL Resolvers, HTTP Interceptors, and View Models. - Dependencies: Depends on the Application layer to execute use cases.

docs.title: 4. Infrastructure Layer
docs.text: Implements the interfaces defined in the Domain layer and handles all external I/O. - Contains: Prisma database repositories, FCM push notification services, Redis caching adapters. - Dependencies: Depends on the Application and Domain layers to know what interfaces to implement.

docs.title: Dependency Rule
docs.text: Source code dependencies must only point inward, toward higher-level policies. Nothing in an inner circle can know anything at all about something in an outer circle.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: To maintain a high quality, readable, and consistent codebase across the entire Halal-Queue engineering team.

docs.title: TypeScript (Backend)
docs.text:
1. Strict Typing: strict mode must be enabled in tsconfig.json. Do not use any; use unknown if the type is truly unknown, or define an interface.
  2. Naming Conventions:
  3. PascalCase for Classes, Interfaces, Enums, and Types.
  4. camelCase for variables, functions, and methods.
  5. UPPER_SNAKE_CASE for global constants and environment variables.
  6. File Naming: Use kebab-case with suffixes indicating the file's role (e.g., user.controller.ts, create-user.use-case.ts).
  7. Linting and Formatting: We use ESLint and Prettier. Run npm run lint before committing.

docs.title: React & Vite (Admin Web)
docs.text:
1. Component Design: Prefer functional components with hooks. Keep components focused, modular, and reusable.
  2. State Management: Use TanStack Query (React Query) / SWR for server state; keep client UI state local via useState/useReducer or lightweight stores (e.g., Zustand).
  3. Styling: Adhere to Tailwind CSS and Shadcn UI / Radix primitives. Avoid inline style objects.
  4. Linting & Formatting: Strict ESLint (eslint-plugin-react-hooks) and Prettier configs.

docs.title: React Native & Expo (Mobile)
docs.text:
1. TypeScript & Strict Typing: Strict mode enabled across all screens, hooks, and components.
  2. Component Architecture: Prefer atomic, modular UI components. Avoid massive single-file screen definitions.
  3. List Virtualization: Always use virtualized list components (@shopify/flash-list or FlatList with getItemLayout) for variable/large datasets.
  4. Navigation: Use Expo Router / React Navigation with typed route parameters.
  5. Linting: Standard ESLint with React Native and Expo config plugins.

docs.title: General Principles
docs.text:
• DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself): Extract common logic to shared utilities or base classes, provided it doesn't violate domain boundaries.
  • KISS (Keep It Simple, Stupid): Avoid over-engineering. Write code that is easy to read and understand.
  • Meaningful Names: Variables and functions should reveal their intent without needing comments (e.g., use fetchActiveVendors() instead of getData()).

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: To define a standardized approach for catching, logging, and returning errors across the API and applications.

docs.title: Domain Exceptions
docs.text: The Domain layer should throw meaningful, business-specific exceptions. - Example: ProductOutOfStockException, VendorNotActiveException. - Rule: Domain exceptions must NEVER contain HTTP status codes. The domain knows nothing about the web.

docs.title: Exception Filters (NestJS)
docs.text: A global Exception Filter intercepts Domain exceptions and translates them into appropriate HTTP responses (e.g., mapping ProductOutOfStockException to a 409 Conflict or 400 Bad Request).

docs.title: Standardized Error Responses
docs.text:
All APIs must return errors in a standardized format: 

{
  "error": {
    "code": "VENDOR_NOT_ACTIVE",
    "message": "The requested vendor is currently inactive and cannot accept orders.",
    "timestamp": "2026-07-29T10:00:00Z",
    "path": "/api/v1/orders"
  }
}

docs.title: Graceful Degradation
docs.text: If a network request fails, the mobile application must fail gracefully: 1. Show a meaningful UI state (e.g., an error graphic or fallback state with a "Retry" button). 2. Never display raw unhandled exceptions or JavaScript stack traces to the end user. 3. Wrap top-level screens and feature components in React Error Boundaries. 4. Use centralized API interceptors (Axios/Fetch) to catch 401 Unauthorized errors and trigger smooth session refresh or re-authentication flows.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Ensure system observability to quickly detect, diagnose, and resolve issues in production.

docs.title: Backend Logging (NestJS)
docs.text:
1. JSON Formatting: In production, all logs must be structured as JSON. This allows log aggregators (e.g., Datadog, ELK, CloudWatch) to parse and index log attributes.
  2. Context: Every log must include a correlation ID (e.g., Request ID) to trace a transaction across the monolith.
  3. Log Levels:
  4. ERROR: System failures or unhandled exceptions that require immediate attention.
  5. WARN: Expected errors or anomalies that do not break the system but should be monitored (e.g., invalid user input retries).
  6. INFO: Normal system lifecycle events (startup, graceful shutdown) and significant business events (e.g., order created).
  7. DEBUG: Detailed information strictly for local development or deep troubleshooting. Disabled in production.
  8. Sensitive Data (PII/PCI): Never log passwords, tokens, full credit card numbers, or sensitive user data. Passwords and tokens must be masked.

docs.title: Key Metrics
docs.text: The system exposes a /metrics endpoint (Prometheus format) to track: 1. HTTP Metrics: Request counts, error rates (4xx, 5xx), and latency (P95, P99). 2. Database Metrics: Connection pool health, query latency, and slow queries. 3. Queue Metrics (BullMQ/Redis): Number of pending jobs, failed jobs, and processing latency for background tasks (e.g., notifications).

docs.title: Health Checks
docs.text: A /health endpoint is available to infrastructure load balancers. It verifies: - Database connectivity - Redis connectivity - Overall memory/CPU bounds

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: To ensure code reliability, prevent regressions, and enforce business rules through automated verification.

docs.title: 1. Unit Tests
docs.text:
• Scope: Individual classes, functions, and Domain layer rules.
  • Tools: Jest.
  • Rule: Domain entities and use cases must have near 100% test coverage. Mocks should be used for all external dependencies (Repositories, Services).

docs.title: 2. Integration Tests
docs.text:
• Scope: Testing the interaction between the Application layer and the Infrastructure layer (e.g., database queries).
  • Tools: Jest, Testcontainers (or an isolated local database).
  • Rule: Validate that Prisma repositories correctly fetch and store data against a real database schema.

docs.title: 3. End-to-End (E2E) Tests
docs.text:
• Scope: Full request lifecycle from the HTTP Controller, through the Use Case, to the Database, and back to the HTTP Response.
  • Tools: Supertest, Jest.
  • Rule: Focus on the happy paths and critical failure paths of the API endpoints. Ensure correct HTTP status codes are returned.

docs.title: 1. Unit & Component Tests
docs.text:
• Scope: Reusable components, custom hooks, utilities, and form validation schemas.
  • Tools: Vitest, React Testing Library.
  • Rule: Validate component interaction, accessible roles, and proper rendering under success/error states.

docs.title: 2. End-to-End (E2E) Tests
docs.text:
• Scope: Critical user journeys (admin login, vendor review/approval, catalog modification).
  • Tools: Playwright or Cypress.

docs.title: 1. Unit Tests
docs.text:
• Scope: Custom hooks, data mappers, utility classes, and pure business logic.
  • Tools: Jest.
  • Rule: Ensure state transformations and validation routines execute deterministically without mounting native views.

docs.title: 2. Component Tests
docs.text:
• Scope: Screen layouts and atomic UI components.
  • Tools: React Native Testing Library (@testing-library/react-native).
  • Rule: Verify that screens correctly render for given prop/query states and user touch interactions emit expected actions.

docs.title: 3. Integration & E2E Tests
docs.text:
• Scope: Core end-to-end user flows (e.g., browse vendor, add to cart, checkout, vendor accept order, scan pickup QR).
  • Tools: Maestro or Detox.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Define a standard branching and contribution model to ensure code quality and a clean project history.

docs.title: Branching Strategy (Trunk-Based Development)
docs.text:
We follow a modified trunk-based development strategy.

  1. main Branch:
  2. The single source of truth.
  3. Must always be deployable.

  4. Direct commits to main are strictly forbidden. All changes must go through a Pull Request.

  5. Feature Branches:

  6. Created from main.
  7. Naming convention: type/issue-number-short-description
  8. Types: feat, fix, chore, docs, refactor.
  9. Example: feat/HQ-102-add-product-variations

docs.title: Commit Conventions
docs.text:
We strictly follow Conventional Commits:

<type>[optional scope]: <description>

[optional body]

[optional footer(s)]
  • feat: A new feature
  • fix: A bug fix
  • docs: Documentation only changes
  • style: Changes that do not affect the meaning of the code (white-space, formatting, etc.)
  • refactor: A code change that neither fixes a bug nor adds a feature
  • test: Adding missing tests or correcting existing tests
  • chore: Changes to the build process or auxiliary tools and libraries

docs.title: Pull Request (PR) Rules
docs.text:
1. Rebase: Feature branches must be rebased against main before opening a PR to avoid merge commits and maintain a linear history.
  2. Review: All PRs require at least one approval from a code owner.
  3. CI Checks: All automated tests, linters, and build checks must pass before a PR can be merged.
  4. Squash and Merge: PRs are squashed into a single commit when merged into main. The squash commit message must follow the Conventional Commits format.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: To outline the daily development practices, code review expectations, and general guidelines for writing software for Halal-Queue.

docs.title: Before Writing Code
docs.text:
1. Read the Documentation: Familiarize yourself with the business rules, system design, and the specific ADRs relevant to your task.
  2. Check for Existing Patterns: If you need to build a new feature (e.g., adding a new entity), look at how similar entities are built within the codebase. Do not reinvent the wheel.
  3. Clarify Requirements: If a business rule is ambiguous, do not guess. Ask the product owner or the software architect.

docs.title: Code Review Expectations
docs.text:
When reviewing code, look for:

  1. Correctness: Does the code fulfill the requirements and edge cases?
  2. Architecture: Does the code respect the Clean Architecture boundaries? (e.g., ensure no database logic exists in the presentation controllers).
  3. Testing: Are there adequate unit and integration tests? Do they test failure scenarios, not just the happy path?
  4. Readability: Is the code easy to understand? Are variables named sensibly?
  5. Security: Are inputs validated? Is authorization enforced properly?

docs.title: Definition of Done (DoD)
docs.text: A task is considered "Done" when: - The code is written and meets the coding standards. - Unit and integration tests are written and passing. - The CI pipeline executes successfully. - Code has been reviewed and approved by at least one peer. - The OpenAPI specification has been updated (if API endpoints were modified). - Any relevant business rules or architecture documents have been updated. - The code is merged into main.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: To ensure that all third-party libraries and tools used in the project are secure, maintained, and do not introduce unnecessary bloat or risk.

docs.title: General Rules
docs.text:
1. Minimal Dependencies: Before adding a new dependency, ask: "Can this be easily implemented using native language features?" Avoid adding large libraries for trivial functions (e.g., using lodash just to capitalize a string).
  2. Approval: Any new dependency that interacts with external services, introduces a new architectural pattern, or is larger than 1MB must be approved by the Architecture Team.
  3. Security: All dependencies must be audited for security vulnerabilities. Run npm audit frequently.
  4. Licensing: Only libraries with permissive open-source licenses (MIT, Apache 2.0, BSD) are allowed. GPL or similarly viral licenses are strictly prohibited.

docs.title: Web (React + Vite) & Backend (NestJS)
docs.text:
• Use pnpm (or npm) monorepo package management consistently.
  • Always lock dependency versions with lockfiles (pnpm-lock.yaml or package-lock.json).
  • Keep dependencies (runtime) and devDependencies (build/test/types) cleanly separated.

docs.title: Mobile (React Native / Expo)
docs.text:
• Use Expo CLI (npx expo install <package>) to install compatible package versions aligned with the active Expo SDK version.
  • Avoid installing unverified native packages requiring custom native code linking without verifying compatibility with Expo config plugins.
  • Ensure dependencies are locked and tracked within the monorepo workspace.

docs.title: Dependency Updates
docs.text:
• Minor and Patch Updates: Should be applied regularly to receive bug fixes and security patches. Dependabot or Renovate should be configured to open PRs for these automatically.
  • Major Updates: Require careful review, testing, and sometimes an explicit upgrade guide in the Architecture Governance section.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: To define how application settings, environment variables, and secrets are managed across different environments (Development, Staging, Production).

docs.title: Core Principles
docs.text:
1. Twelve-Factor App: We follow the 12-Factor App methodology. Configuration that varies between environments must be stored in the environment, not in the codebase.
  2. No Secrets in Source Control: Never commit .env files, API keys, passwords, or certificates to Git.
  3. Type Safety: Backend configuration loaded from the environment must be validated and typed upon application startup.

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
• Local development uses a .env file (which is ignored by .gitignore).
  • A .env.example file should be maintained with placeholder values to show required variables.

docs.title: NestJS ConfigService
docs.text:
• Use the @nestjs/config module to load and validate environment variables.
  • Define a strict schema (e.g., using Joi or class-validator) to ensure the application fails to start if a required environment variable is missing or malformed.

Example variables: - DATABASE_URL - REDIS_URL - JWT_SECRET - PORT

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
• Environment variables exposed to client-side code must use the VITE_ prefix (e.g., VITE_API_URL, VITE_APP_ENV).
  • Variables are accessed safely via import.meta.env.VITE_*.
  • Stored locally in .env.local (git-ignored) and injected via CI/CD for staging and production builds.

docs.title: App Config & Environment Profiles
docs.text: The React Native mobile applications use dynamic configuration (app.config.ts or app.json) along with EAS environment secrets: - Configuration profiles are managed for development, staging, and production. - Environment variables are accessed via expo-constants (Constants.expoConfig.extra) or process.env. - Native keys (e.g., Google Maps API keys, bundle identifiers) are securely injected through app.config.ts during EAS build workflows and never committed in plaintext.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: To ensure the Halal-Queue platform remains responsive, highly available, and resource-efficient as it scales.

docs.title: Database Operations
docs.text:
1. N+1 Problem: Always use include (Prisma) or proper JOINs to fetch related data. Never loop over a result set and execute a query for each item.
  2. Indexes: Ensure all frequently queried columns, foreign keys, and sorting columns have appropriate database indexes.
  3. Pagination: Never return unbounded lists. All list endpoints must support and enforce pagination (Limit/Offset or Cursor-based).

docs.title: Caching
docs.text:
• Redis: Use Redis to cache read-heavy, infrequently changing data (e.g., Active Global Products, Vendor Operating Hours).
  • Cache Invalidation: Implement precise cache invalidation strategies triggered by Domain Events when the underlying data changes.

docs.title: Asynchronous Processing
docs.text: • BullMQ: Do not perform long-running tasks synchronously in an HTTP request. Offload tasks like sending emails, generating reports, or pushing FCM notifications to background queues using BullMQ.

docs.title: UI Rendering & Reconciliation
docs.text:
1. Prevent Unnecessary Re-renders: Use React.memo, useCallback, and useMemo deliberately around performance-critical lists and interactive controls.
  2. Virtualized Lists: Use @shopify/flash-list or FlatList with windowSize and maxToRenderPerBatch tuned. Never map arrays of unbounded items directly inside a ScrollView.
  3. Native Driver Animations: Ensure all UI animations run on the UI thread using react-native-reanimated instead of blocking the JavaScript bridge thread.

docs.title: Network & Assets
docs.text:
1. Image Caching & Prefetching: Use expo-image for high-performance image caching, memory management, and smooth placeholder transitions.
  2. Debouncing: Debounce rapid user inputs (e.g., search queries) by 300ms to avoid unnecessary API round-trips.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: To define the process for making, reviewing, and recording significant architectural changes within the Halal-Queue project.

docs.title: Architecture Decision Records (ADRs)
docs.text: We use ADRs to capture architectural decisions made along with their context and consequences.

docs.title: When to write an ADR
docs.text: Write an ADR when a decision: - Introduces a new technology or framework (e.g., choosing PostgreSQL). - Changes the overall structure of the application (e.g., moving from a monolith to microservices). - Significantly affects non-functional requirements (security, performance, scalability).

docs.title: ADR Process
docs.text:
1. Draft: A developer proposes an architectural change by writing a draft ADR using the standard template (docs/templates/adr-template.md).
  2. Review: The team reviews the proposal via a Pull Request. Discussions happen on the PR.
  3. Approve/Reject: The Software Architect or Tech Lead approves or rejects the ADR.
  4. Record: Once approved, the ADR is merged into docs/adr/ and becomes the official stance of the project.

docs.title: Code Reviews
docs.text: Architecture is primarily enforced through peer code reviews. Reviewers must ensure that code complies with Clean Architecture boundaries and SOLID principles.

docs.title: Linting and Tooling
docs.text: Where possible, architectural boundaries should be enforced via tooling: - ESLint: Use boundary-enforcement rules (e.g., @nx/enforce-module-boundaries if using Nx, or standard import restrictions) to prevent the domain layer from importing from infrastructure.

docs.title: Technical Debt
docs.text: When an architectural compromise is made for the sake of speed (a "hack"), it must be documented with a TODO comment linking to a tracking ticket to pay down the technical debt.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
This directory contains the system design documentation for the Halal-Queue platform.

These documents transform the approved business requirements into a comprehensive technical design that guides implementation. They define the system architecture, data model, interfaces, security, deployment, and operational behavior while remaining independent of source code implementation details.

The system design serves as the bridge between the business documentation and the software architecture documentation.

docs.title: Design Goals
docs.text:
The system design aims to provide:

  • Clear architectural boundaries
  • Well-defined business modules
  • Consistent implementation guidance
  • High maintainability
  • Reliable and secure operations
  • Scalability for future growth
  • Traceability from business requirements to implementation
  • Technology-aligned architecture documentation

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
The system design defines:

  • Business module boundaries
  • High-level system architecture
  • Domain model
  • Entity relationships
  • Business workflows
  • API design principles
  • Database architecture
  • Security architecture
  • Deployment architecture

The system design does not define:

  • Source code organization
  • Programming conventions
  • Framework-specific implementation
  • CI/CD pipelines
  • Development workflow

These topics are covered in the Software Architecture documentation.

docs.title: Document Index
docs.text: No. Document Purpose 01 Domain Model Defines the core business domain, aggregates, entities, and relationships. 02 Entity Relationship Model Defines the conceptual data model and entity relationships. 03 State Machines Defines lifecycle states and valid transitions for major business entities. 04 Sequence Diagrams Describes interactions between users, applications, and backend services. 05 System Architecture Defines the overall application architecture, business modules, and system components. 06 API Design Defines API architecture, conventions, and integration patterns. 07 Database Design Defines the logical database architecture and persistence strategy. 08 Security Architecture Defines authentication, authorization, and security controls. 09 Deployment Architecture Defines deployment topology, infrastructure, and runtime environment.

docs.title: Architectural Principles
docs.text:
The Halal-Queue platform follows these architectural principles:

  • Modular Monolith architecture
  • Dedicated background worker for asynchronous processing
  • Domain-driven module boundaries
  • Separation of concerns
  • Stateless REST APIs
  • Event-driven background processing
  • Secure by default
  • Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)
  • Scalability through modular design
  • Future-ready for microservice decomposition

docs.title: Core Business Modules
docs.text:
The backend is organized into independent business modules.

Module Responsibility Authentication Registration, login, OTP verification, password management Authorization Roles, permissions, access control Profile User profile management Vendor Vendors, branches, operating hours, business profile Catalog Categories, products, vendor listings, availability Ordering Cart, orders, order modifications Pickup Pickup workflow and verification Notification Push notifications and notification history

Each module owns its business logic and communicates through well-defined service interfaces.

docs.title: System Characteristics
docs.text:
Version 1 provides:

  • One NestJS backend application
  • One Worker application
  • One PostgreSQL database
  • One Redis instance
  • One BullMQ job queue
  • One object storage service
  • Multiple client applications
  • Modular business domains
  • Stateless REST APIs
  • Real-time communication using WebSocket
  • Background job processing

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
This document defines the core business entities of the Halal-Queue platform and the relationships between them.

The Domain Model is a conceptual representation of the business. It is independent of database design, APIs, programming languages, or implementation details.

docs.title: Design Principles
docs.text:
The domain model follows these principles:

  • Represent business concepts, not database tables.
  • Keep entities independent and loosely coupled.
  • Model relationships explicitly.
  • Avoid duplication of responsibilities.
  • Support future platform growth without major redesign.

docs.title: Core Domains
docs.text:
The platform consists of the following domains:

Identity

Vendor Management

Catalog

Ordering

Pickup

Notifications

docs.title: Identity
docs.text:
Represents every authenticated platform user.

Examples:

  • Customer
  • Vendor Owner
  • Platform Administrator

Responsibilities:

  • Authentication
  • Authorization
  • Profile
  • Security

docs.title: Vendor
docs.text:
Represents a business registered on the platform.

Responsibilities:

  • Business Profile
  • Branch Management
  • Product Management

A Vendor may own multiple Branches.

docs.title: Branch
docs.text:
Represents a physical store location.

Responsibilities:

  • Pickup Orders
  • Operating Hours
  • Product Availability

Every Branch belongs to one Vendor.

docs.title: Product
docs.text:
Represents an item offered for sale.

Examples:

  • Milk
  • Rice
  • Bread
  • Eggs

Products belong to a Branch.

docs.title: Product Availability
docs.text:
Represents whether customers may currently order a Product.

States:

  • Available
  • Unavailable

Availability is controlled by the Vendor.

docs.title: Customer
docs.text:
Represents an Identity that places orders.

A Customer may create many Orders.

docs.title: Order
docs.text:
Represents a customer's purchase request.

Responsibilities:

  • Order Status
  • Pickup
  • Total Amount
  • Customer Reference

An Order contains one or more Order Items.

docs.title: Order Item
docs.text:
Represents a single product within an Order.

Responsibilities:

  • Product
  • Quantity
  • Price
  • Status

Order Items are managed independently.

docs.title: Pickup
docs.text:
Represents the collection of an Order.

Responsibilities:

  • Pickup Code
  • Pickup Status
  • Verification
  • Completion

Every Order has exactly one Pickup.

docs.title: Notification
docs.text:
Represents a message sent by the platform.

Examples:

  • OTP
  • Order Confirmed
  • Ready for Pickup
  • Order Change Request

Notifications are associated with an Identity.

docs.text:
Identity

docs.text:

docs.text:
This document defines the conceptual entities of the Halal-Queue platform and the relationships between them.

The Entity Relationship Model (ERM) translates the Domain Model into entities and relationships while remaining independent of physical database implementation.

This document intentionally avoids database-specific concerns such as column types, indexes, or SQL syntax.

docs.title: Design Principles

  • One Identity represents one platform account.
  • Business roles are assigned through Profiles.
  • Relationships explicitly describe ownership and references.
  • Entities represent business concepts, not implementation details.
  • Cardinality is defined for every relationship.

docs.title: Identity-Centric Design
docs.text:
Authentication is always performed against the Identity entity.

Profiles extend the Identity with business-specific capabilities.

This allows a single person to:

  • Shop as a customer.
  • Own one or more grocery stores.
  • Access administrative features if granted.

without creating multiple accounts.

docs.title: Product Availability
docs.text:
Availability is modeled separately from Product.

This allows a product to remain visible while temporarily unavailable without changing catalog information.

docs.title: Pickup
docs.text:
Pickup is modeled independently from Order.

This allows the pickup lifecycle and verification process to evolve without affecting order management.

docs.title: Design Principles

  • Record significant state changes for auditing.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
This document defines the high-level architecture of the Halal-Queue platform.

It describes the major software components, their responsibilities, and how they interact while remaining maintainable, scalable, and loosely coupled.

Version 1 adopts a Modular Monolith with a Dedicated Background Worker.

docs.title: Architectural Goals
docs.text:
The architecture is designed to provide:

  • Clear module boundaries
  • High maintainability
  • Separation of concerns
  • Secure authentication and authorization
  • Reliable order processing
  • Efficient asynchronous processing
  • Horizontal scalability
  • Future migration to microservices if required

docs.title: Architecture Style
docs.text:
Version 1 uses:

Modular Monolith
+
Dedicated Background Worker

Characteristics:

  • One backend application
  • One worker application
  • One PostgreSQL database
  • One Redis instance
  • Multiple independent business modules
  • Asynchronous background processing using BullMQ

docs.title: Module Communication
docs.text:
Business modules communicate internally through service interfaces.

Communication mechanisms include:

  • Internal service calls
  • REST APIs
  • WebSocket events
  • BullMQ background jobs

        ▼

        │

Modules shall never access another module's persistence layer directly.

docs.title: Security Architecture
docs.text:
Authentication:

  • Phone number
  • OTP verification
  • Password
  • JWT Access Token
  • Refresh Token

Authorization:

  • Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)

Password Storage:

  • Argon2id password hashing

Communication:

  • HTTPS only
  • Secure WebSocket connections

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
All modules shall follow a consistent error-handling strategy.

Error categories include:

  • Validation errors
  • Authentication errors
  • Authorization errors
  • Business rule violations
  • Resource not found
  • Conflict errors
  • System errors

All REST APIs shall return standardized error responses.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
The platform shall log:

  • Authentication events
  • Authorization failures
  • Business events
  • API requests
  • Worker execution
  • Queue failures
  • System errors
  • Security events

Sensitive information shall never be written to logs.

docs.title: Scalability
docs.text:
The architecture supports future decomposition into independent services.

Possible future services include:

  • Authentication Service
  • Vendor Service
  • Catalog Service
  • Ordering Service
  • Pickup Service
  • Notification Service
  • Worker Service

The business modules defined in Version 1 establish the future service boundaries.

  • API Gateway

  • Multiple backend instances
  • CDN

docs.title: Architectural Principles
docs.text:
The platform follows these principles:

  • Modular Monolith architecture
  • Domain-driven module boundaries
  • Separation of concerns
  • Single Responsibility Principle
  • Dependency Inversion Principle
  • Stateless REST APIs
  • Secure by default
  • Asynchronous processing where appropriate
  • Scalability through modular design

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
This document defines the API architecture, design principles, standards, and conventions for the Halal-Queue platform.

The API serves as the communication layer between client applications and the backend while ensuring consistency, security, maintainability, and future extensibility.

docs.title: Design Goals
docs.text:
The API shall provide:

  • Consistent request and response formats
  • Stateless communication
  • Secure authentication and authorization
  • Clear resource-oriented endpoints
  • Standardized error handling
  • Versioning support
  • Real-time updates
  • Backward compatibility

docs.title: API Architecture
docs.text:
Version 1 uses:

  • REST APIs
  • JSON request and response bodies
  • HTTPS
  • JWT Authentication
  • WebSocket for real-time updates

The backend exposes a single API consumed by:

  • Customer Mobile Application
  • Vendor Mobile Application
  • Admin Web Application

docs.title: API Versioning
docs.text:
All endpoints shall be versioned.

Example:

/api/v1/

Future breaking changes shall introduce a new major version.

Example:

/api/v2/

docs.title: API Style
docs.text:
The API follows REST principles.

Resources are represented by nouns rather than verbs.

Examples:

GET    /api/v1/orders

POST   /api/v1/orders

GET    /api/v1/orders/{orderId}

PATCH  /api/v1/orders/{orderId}

DELETE /api/v1/orders/{orderId}

Avoid action-oriented endpoints such as:

/createOrder

/updateVendor

/deleteProduct

docs.title: API Modules
docs.text:
Endpoints are organized by business domain.

Module Base Path Authentication /api/v1/auth Customers /api/v1/customers Vendors /api/v1/vendors Catalog /api/v1/catalog Cart /api/v1/cart Orders /api/v1/orders Pickup /api/v1/pickup Notifications /api/v1/notifications Admin /api/v1/admin Uploads /api/v1/uploads

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Version 1 supports:

  • Phone Number Registration
  • OTP Verification
  • Password Login
  • JWT Access Token
  • Refresh Token

Authentication flow:

Register

↓

Receive OTP

↓

Verify OTP

↓

Set Password

↓

Login

↓

Receive JWT Tokens

↓

Authenticated Requests

docs.title: Authorization
docs.text:
Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) is used.

Supported roles:

  • Customer
  • Vendor
  • Vendor Staff (Future)
  • Administrator

Each endpoint defines the roles permitted to access it.

docs.title: HTTP Methods
docs.text:
Method Purpose GET Retrieve resources POST Create resources PUT Replace resources PATCH Partial update DELETE Delete resources

PATCH should be preferred over PUT for partial updates.

docs.title: Request Format
docs.text:
Requests shall use JSON.

Example:

{
  "phoneNumber": "+12125551234",
  "password": "********"
}

File uploads use multipart/form-data.

docs.title: Response Format
docs.text:
All successful responses follow a standard format.

Example:

{
  "success": true,
  "message": "Order created successfully.",
  "data": {
    "orderId": "ORD-100001"
  }
}

docs.title: Pagination
docs.text:
Collection endpoints shall support pagination.

Example:

GET /api/v1/orders?page=1&pageSize=20

Response:

{
  "success": true,
  "message": "Orders retrieved successfully.",
  "data": [],
  "meta": {
    "page": 1,
    "pageSize": 20,
    "totalItems": 250,
    "totalPages": 13
  }
}

docs.title: Filtering
docs.text:
Collection endpoints may support filtering.

Example:

GET /api/v1/catalog/products?categoryId=12

GET /api/v1/orders?status=READY

GET /api/v1/vendors?status=OPEN

docs.title: Searching
docs.text:
Resources may support search.

Example:

GET /api/v1/catalog/products?search=rice

docs.title: Sorting
docs.text:
Resources may support sorting.

Examples:

sort=name

sort=price

sort=-price

sort=createdAt

docs.title: HTTP Status Codes
docs.text: Status Meaning 200 Success 201 Created 204 No Content 400 Bad Request 401 Unauthorized 403 Forbidden 404 Not Found 409 Conflict 422 Validation Error 429 Too Many Requests 500 Internal Server Error

docs.title: Error Response
docs.text:
All errors follow a standard format.

Example:

{
  "success": false,
  "message": "Validation failed.",
  "errors": [
    {
      "field": "phoneNumber",
      "code": "INVALID_PHONE_NUMBER",
      "message": "Phone number is invalid."
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Requests shall be validated before business logic executes.

Validation includes:

  • Required fields
  • Data types
  • Value ranges
  • Phone number format
  • String length
  • Business rules

Invalid requests return HTTP 422.

docs.title: File Upload
docs.text:
Image uploads use dedicated endpoints.

Example:

POST /api/v1/uploads/images

Supported files:

  • Product images
  • Vendor logos
  • Business images
  • Profile images

Uploaded files are stored in S3-compatible object storage.

docs.title: Real-Time Communication
docs.text:
Real-time updates use WebSocket.

Typical events include:

  • Order Created
  • Order Accepted
  • Order Ready
  • Pickup Completed
  • Notification Created

WebSocket is used only for server-to-client events.

Business operations continue to use REST APIs.

docs.title: Background Processing
docs.text:
Long-running operations are processed asynchronously.

Examples:

  • Push notification delivery
  • Scheduled jobs
  • Daily product availability reset
  • Retry processing

Background jobs are queued using BullMQ and executed by the Worker application.

docs.title: Idempotency
docs.text:
The following operations should be idempotent where applicable:

  • OTP resend
  • Refresh token
  • Retry background jobs

Duplicate client requests should not create duplicate resources.

docs.title: Rate Limiting
docs.text:
Sensitive endpoints should be rate limited.

Examples:

  • Registration
  • OTP requests
  • Login
  • Password reset

Rate limits protect against abuse and brute-force attacks.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
All API communication shall use HTTPS.

Security measures include:

  • JWT Authentication
  • Refresh Tokens
  • RBAC
  • Input validation
  • Output sanitization
  • CORS
  • Rate limiting

Sensitive information shall never be returned in API responses.

docs.title: API Documentation
docs.text:
The OpenAPI specification is the authoritative API contract.

Location:

openapi/
└── openapi.yaml

The specification defines:

  • Endpoints
  • Schemas
  • Request bodies
  • Responses
  • Authentication
  • Error responses

Client SDKs and API documentation may be generated from this specification.

docs.title: API Evolution Policy
docs.text:
The API follows backward compatibility principles.

Allowed changes within the same major version:

  • Add new endpoints
  • Add optional request fields
  • Add optional response fields
  • Improve documentation

Breaking changes require a new API version.

Examples of breaking changes:

  • Removing endpoints
  • Removing response fields
  • Changing field data types
  • Changing authentication mechanisms

docs.title: Out of Scope
docs.text:
This document does not define:

  • Individual endpoint specifications
  • Business workflows
  • Database schema
  • Internal module implementation
  • Client application logic

These topics are documented separately.

docs.text: Version Date Author Changes 1.0.0 2026-07-28 Software Architecture Team Initial version

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
This document defines the logical database architecture for the Halal-Queue platform.

It describes the platform's persistence strategy, data ownership, integrity rules, storage technologies, and architectural principles. It intentionally remains independent of the physical database schema and implementation details.

Detailed table definitions, migrations, and ORM models are maintained separately within the implementation repository.

docs.title: Design Goals
docs.text:
The database architecture shall provide:

  • Data integrity
  • Strong consistency
  • Reliable transactions
  • Efficient querying
  • High maintainability
  • Scalability
  • Auditability
  • Clear ownership of business data

docs.title: Database Technologies
docs.text: Component Technology Primary Database PostgreSQL ORM Prisma ORM Cache Redis Background Jobs BullMQ Object Storage MinIO (Development) / AWS S3 (Production)

docs.title: Database Architecture
docs.text:
NestJS Backend
                           │
          ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
          ▼                ▼                ▼
     PostgreSQL         Redis         Object Storage
                            │          (MinIO / AWS S3)
                            ▼
                         BullMQ
                            │
                            ▼
                    Worker Application

docs.title: Persistence Strategy
docs.text:
The platform uses PostgreSQL as the system of record for all business data.

Business entities are stored using a normalized relational model while maintaining transactional consistency and referential integrity.

Redis stores temporary application data and supports asynchronous processing.

Object Storage stores uploaded files that are referenced from PostgreSQL.

docs.title: Data Ownership
docs.text:
Each business module owns its data.

Modules shall never modify another module's data directly.

Module Owns Authentication Identity, OTP Verification, Refresh Tokens Profile Customer Profiles Vendor Vendors, Branches, Operating Hours Catalog Categories, Global Products, Vendor Product Listings, Product Availability Ordering Cart, Orders, Order Items, Order Change Requests Pickup Pickup Records Notification Notifications

Communication between modules shall occur through application services rather than direct database access.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Owns:

  • Identity
  • Phone Number
  • Password Hash
  • Refresh Tokens
  • OTP Verification

docs.title: Profile
docs.text:
Owns:

  • Customer Profile
  • Vendor Owner Profile
  • Personal Information

docs.title: Vendor
docs.text:
Owns:

  • Vendor
  • Branch
  • Operating Hours
  • Temporary Closures
  • Vendor Status

Business profile information is maintained as part of the Vendor aggregate.

docs.title: Catalog
docs.text:
Owns:

  • Categories
  • Global Products
  • Vendor Product Listings
  • Product Availability

The platform maintains a shared product catalog.

Each vendor publishes its own listing for products it offers.

Product availability is managed independently for each vendor listing.

docs.title: Ordering
docs.text:
Owns:

  • Cart
  • Orders
  • Order Items
  • Order Change Requests

Orders remain immutable except through defined business workflows.

docs.title: Pickup
docs.text:
Owns:

  • Pickup Records
  • Pickup Codes
  • Pickup Verification

Pickup information is permanently associated with its order.

docs.title: Notification
docs.text:
Owns:

  • Notification History
  • Delivery Status
  • Read Status

Notification delivery is processed asynchronously.

docs.title: Product Availability
docs.text:
The platform does not maintain inventory quantities.

Each vendor product listing has an availability status.

Supported states include:

  • Available
  • Unavailable

Business rules:

  • Vendors may mark products as unavailable.
  • Products marked unavailable automatically become available during the next scheduled daily reset.
  • If a product becomes unavailable after an order is placed, the vendor may:
  • Mark the ordered item as unavailable with a note.
  • Propose a reduced quantity.
  • Customers may:
  • Accept the proposed change.
  • Cancel the affected item.
  • Cancel the entire order.

The daily availability reset is executed by the Worker application.

docs.title: Redis
docs.text:
Redis stores temporary application data.

Typical use cases include:

  • Distributed cache
  • Queue backend
  • Temporary application state
  • Future session storage
  • Rate limiting

Redis is not the source of truth for business data.

docs.title: Background Jobs
docs.text:
BullMQ manages asynchronous processing.

Typical jobs include:

  • Push notification delivery
  • Daily product availability reset
  • Scheduled tasks
  • Retry processing

Jobs are processed by the Worker application.

docs.title: Object Storage
docs.text:
Object Storage stores uploaded files.

Examples include:

  • Product images
  • Vendor logos
  • Business images
  • Profile images

Business records store only the object key or public URL.

docs.title: Shared Entity Fields
docs.text:
Most persistent entities should include common audit fields.

Field Purpose id Primary identifier created_at Creation timestamp updated_at Last modification timestamp created_by Creator (optional) updated_by Last modifier (optional)

Additional audit fields may be introduced where required.

docs.title: Identifier Strategy
docs.text:
Internal identifiers use UUID values.

Business identifiers remain human-readable.

Examples:

Entity Example Vendor VEN-100001 Order ORD-100001 Pickup PUP-100001

Business identifiers are intended for users, while UUIDs are used internally.

docs.title: Data Integrity
docs.text:
Integrity is enforced through:

  • Primary keys
  • Foreign keys
  • Unique constraints
  • Check constraints
  • Database transactions
  • Application validation

Business rules are enforced within the application layer.

docs.title: Transaction Management
docs.text:
Database transactions are required for operations including:

  • User registration
  • Vendor registration
  • Order placement
  • Order modification
  • Order acceptance
  • Pickup verification
  • Pickup completion

Transactions should remain short-lived to maximize concurrency.

docs.title: Soft Delete Strategy
docs.text:
Soft deletion is used where historical records should remain available.

Typical examples include:

  • Vendors
  • Branches
  • Vendor Product Listings

Business history such as Orders and Pickups shall never be deleted.

docs.title: Indexing Strategy
docs.text:
Indexes should be created for:

  • Primary keys
  • Foreign keys
  • Phone numbers
  • Business identifiers
  • Frequently searched columns
  • Frequently filtered columns
  • Frequently sorted columns

Indexes should be reviewed regularly to balance query performance and write performance.

docs.title: PostgreSQL
docs.text:
• Automated daily backups
  • Point-in-time recovery
  • Transaction log archiving

docs.title: Redis
docs.text:
• Persistence enabled
  • Rebuilt from PostgreSQL where applicable

docs.title: Object Storage
docs.text:
• Versioning
  • Replication (Production)
  • Regular backup verification

docs.title: Performance Strategy
docs.text:
Database performance is improved through:

  • Proper indexing
  • Query optimization
  • Pagination
  • Connection pooling
  • Redis caching
  • Efficient transaction boundaries

docs.title: Future Evolution
docs.text:
Future versions may introduce:

  • Read replicas
  • Database partitioning
  • Full-text search
  • Analytics database
  • Data warehouse
  • Event sourcing for selected modules

The logical data model is designed to support future architectural evolution without major redesign.

docs.title: Out of Scope
docs.text:
This document does not define:

  • Physical database schema
  • Prisma models
  • Migration scripts
  • SQL DDL
  • Seed data
  • Backup implementation
  • Database administration procedures

These artifacts are maintained within the implementation repository.

docs.text: Version Date Author Changes 1.0.0 2026-07-28 Software Architecture Team Initial version

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
This document defines the security architecture for the Halal-Queue platform.

It describes the authentication model, authorization model, data protection strategy, communication security, operational security controls, and business security rules used throughout the platform.

The objective is to protect customer data, vendor data, business operations, and platform infrastructure while maintaining usability and scalability.

docs.title: Security Goals
docs.text:
The platform shall provide:

  • Confidentiality
  • Integrity
  • Availability
  • Authentication
  • Authorization
  • Privacy
  • Auditability
  • Secure communications

docs.title: Security Principles
docs.text:
The platform follows these principles:

  • Secure by Default
  • Least Privilege
  • Defense in Depth
  • Zero Trust
  • Fail Secure
  • Separation of Duties
  • Principle of Minimum Exposure

Security controls shall be applied consistently across all applications.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Version 1 supports:

  • Phone Number Registration
  • SMS OTP Verification
  • Password Authentication
  • JWT Access Tokens
  • Refresh Tokens

Authentication flow:

Register
      │
Receive OTP
      │
Verify OTP
      │
Set Password
      │
Login
      │
Receive Tokens

Only verified phone numbers may create accounts.

docs.title: Authorization
docs.text:
The platform uses Role-Based Access Control (RBAC).

Supported roles:

  • Customer
  • Vendor
  • Administrator

Every API endpoint explicitly defines the roles permitted to access it.

Authorization is enforced by the backend for every request.

docs.title: Business Security Rules
docs.text:
The platform enforces business-level authorization in addition to role checks.

Examples include:

  • Customers may access only their own orders.
  • Customers may access only their own profile.
  • Vendors may manage only their own business.
  • Vendors may manage only their own branches.
  • Vendors may manage only their own product listings.
  • Vendors may access only orders belonging to their branches.
  • Vendors may verify pickup only for their own orders.
  • Administrators have platform-wide administrative access.
  • Pickup codes are single-use.
  • Completed orders cannot be modified.
  • Vendors cannot modify another vendor's information.

docs.title: Password Security
docs.text:
Passwords shall:

  • Never be stored in plain text.
  • Be hashed using Argon2id.
  • Never be returned by APIs.
  • Never be logged.
  • Never be reversible.

Password complexity requirements are enforced during registration and password changes.

docs.title: JWT Security
docs.text:
Authentication uses:

  • Short-lived Access Tokens
  • Long-lived Refresh Tokens

Access Tokens:

  • Used for API authorization.
  • Sent in the Authorization: Bearer header.
  • Contain only required claims.

Refresh Tokens:

  • Stored securely.
  • Rotated after successful refresh.
  • Revocable.
  • Invalidated during logout.

docs.title: Session Management
docs.text:
The backend uses stateless authentication.

Session information is represented by JWTs.

Refresh token metadata may be stored to support:

  • Logout
  • Token revocation
  • Device management (future)

Expired sessions require re-authentication.

docs.title: OTP Security
docs.text:
OTP verification includes:

  • Expiration time
  • Maximum verification attempts
  • Maximum resend attempts
  • Single-use validation

OTP values:

  • Are never stored in plain text.
  • Are invalid after successful verification.
  • Cannot be reused.

docs.title: API Security
docs.text:
All APIs require:

  • HTTPS
  • JWT Authentication
  • Input Validation
  • Output Sanitization
  • Rate Limiting
  • CORS Protection

Business validation occurs after authentication and authorization.

docs.title: WebSocket Security
docs.text:
WebSocket connections require authentication.

Security requirements include:

  • JWT authentication during connection
  • Authorization before subscribing to private events
  • Connection termination after token expiration
  • Access limited to authorized resources

Typical events include:

  • Order updates
  • Pickup updates
  • Notifications

docs.title: Data Protection
docs.text:
Sensitive information includes:

  • Phone numbers
  • Password hashes
  • Refresh tokens
  • OTP verification data

Sensitive information shall:

  • Never appear in logs.
  • Never appear in error responses.
  • Be encrypted where appropriate.
  • Be accessible only to authorized users.

docs.title: File Upload Security
docs.text:
Uploaded files shall be validated before storage.

Validation includes:

  • File type
  • MIME type
  • File size
  • Extension
  • Virus scanning (future)

Allowed uploads include:

  • Product images
  • Vendor logos
  • Business images
  • Profile images

Executable files are prohibited.

Files are stored in S3-compatible object storage.

docs.title: Rate Limiting
docs.text:
Rate limiting protects public-facing endpoints.

Examples include:

  • Registration
  • OTP requests
  • OTP verification
  • Login
  • Password reset
  • Public catalog requests

Limits shall be configurable.

docs.title: Audit Logging
docs.text:
Security-related events shall be logged.

Examples include:

  • Registration
  • Login
  • Logout
  • Password changes
  • OTP verification
  • Failed authentication
  • Failed authorization
  • Vendor approval
  • Administrative actions

Audit logs shall never contain:

  • Passwords
  • OTP values
  • JWT tokens
  • Refresh tokens

docs.title: Security Headers
docs.text:
Responses should include appropriate security headers.

Examples:

  • Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS)
  • X-Content-Type-Options
  • X-Frame-Options
  • Referrer-Policy
  • Content-Security-Policy (Admin Web)

docs.title: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)
docs.text:
Only approved client applications may access the API.

Production origins shall be explicitly configured.

Credentials shall never be accepted from untrusted origins.

docs.title: Secrets Management
docs.text:
Sensitive configuration includes:

  • JWT signing keys
  • Database credentials
  • Redis credentials
  • Object storage credentials
  • Firebase credentials
  • SMS provider credentials

Secrets shall:

  • Never be committed to source control.
  • Be stored using environment variables or a secrets manager.
  • Be rotated periodically.

docs.title: Dependency Security
docs.text:
Third-party dependencies shall be:

  • Regularly updated
  • Vulnerability scanned
  • Reviewed before adoption
  • Removed when no longer maintained

docs.title: Infrastructure Security
docs.text:
Production infrastructure shall provide:

  • HTTPS termination
  • Firewall protection
  • Private database network
  • Private Redis instance
  • Restricted object storage access
  • Encrypted backups
  • Monitoring and alerting

docs.title: Incident Response
docs.text:
The platform shall support:

  • Security event detection
  • Audit log investigation
  • Token revocation
  • Credential rotation
  • Recovery procedures
  • Post-incident analysis

docs.title: Future Enhancements
docs.text:
Future versions may introduce:

  • Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)
  • Passkeys (WebAuthn)
  • Device management
  • Biometric authentication
  • Single Sign-On (SSO)
  • Hardware security keys
  • Fine-grained permissions beyond RBAC

docs.title: Out of Scope
docs.text:
This document does not define:

  • NestJS implementation details
  • Cloud infrastructure configuration
  • CI/CD security pipelines
  • Operating system hardening
  • Network topology

These topics are covered by implementation and deployment documentation.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
This document defines the deployment architecture for the Halal-Queue platform.

It describes how the software components are deployed, connected, secured, and operated across development, staging, and production environments.

docs.title: Deployment Goals
docs.text:
The deployment architecture shall provide:

  • High availability
  • Reliability
  • Scalability
  • Security
  • Maintainability
  • Observability
  • Disaster recovery

docs.title: Deployment Model
docs.text:
Version 1 uses a modular monolith deployment.

The platform consists of:

  • Customer Mobile Application
  • Vendor iPad Application (iOS only)
  • Admin Web Application
  • Backend API
  • Worker Application
  • PostgreSQL
  • Redis
  • Object Storage
  • Firebase Cloud Messaging
  • SMS OTP Provider

docs.title: High-Level Deployment
docs.text:
Internet
                      │
        ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
        │             │             │
        ▼             ▼             ▼
 Customer App    Vendor App    Admin Web
 React Native   React Native   React + Vite
    (Expo)         (Expo)         (SPA)
        │             │             │
        └─────────────┼─────────────┘
                      │
                 HTTPS / WSS
                      │
              Reverse Proxy / Load Balancer
                      │
        ┌─────────────┴─────────────┐
        │                           │
        ▼                           ▼
   NestJS Backend             Worker Application
        │                           │
        ├──────────────┬────────────┤
        ▼              ▼            ▼
   PostgreSQL       Redis        Object Storage
                        │
                        ▼
                     BullMQ

        │
        ▼

Firebase Cloud Messaging

SMS OTP Provider

docs.title: Customer Mobile
docs.text:
Technology:

  • React Native (Expo)
  • TypeScript

Platforms:

  • Android
  • iOS

docs.title: Vendor Mobile
docs.text:
Technology:

  • React Native (Expo)
  • TypeScript

Platforms:

  • Android
  • iOS (iPad optimized)

docs.title: Admin Web
docs.text:
Technology:

  • React
  • Vite (Single Page Application)
  • TypeScript

Runs in the user's browser (Static SPA hosted on S3/CloudFront or Nginx).

docs.title: Backend
docs.text:
Technology:

  • NestJS

Responsibilities:

  • REST API
  • Authentication
  • Authorization
  • Business logic
  • WebSocket gateway
  • File management

The backend is stateless and horizontally scalable.

docs.title: Worker Application
docs.text:
Technology:

  • NestJS Worker

Responsibilities:

  • BullMQ job processing
  • Push notifications
  • Daily product availability reset
  • Scheduled jobs
  • Retry processing

Workers may be scaled independently of the backend.

docs.title: Database
docs.text:
Technology:

  • PostgreSQL

Responsibilities:

  • Business data
  • Transactions
  • Referential integrity

PostgreSQL is the system of record.

docs.title: Redis
docs.text:
Technology:

  • Redis

Responsibilities:

  • Queue backend
  • Temporary cache
  • Rate limiting
  • Future session storage

Redis is not the source of truth for business data.

docs.title: Object Storage
docs.text:
Technology:

Development:

  • MinIO

Production:

  • AWS S3 (or another S3-compatible service)

Stores:

  • Product images
  • Vendor logos
  • Business images
  • Profile images

docs.title: Push Notifications
docs.text:
Technology:

  • Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM)

Used for:

  • Order updates
  • Pickup notifications
  • General notifications

docs.title: SMS Provider
docs.text:
Provides:

  • OTP delivery
  • Future SMS notifications

The provider is replaceable without changing application logic.

docs.title: Development Environment
docs.text:
Local development typically uses Docker Compose.

Example services:

  • Backend
  • Worker
  • PostgreSQL
  • Redis
  • MinIO

Client applications run locally.

docs.title: Staging Environment
docs.text:
The staging environment mirrors production as closely as practical.

Used for:

  • QA testing
  • User acceptance testing
  • Performance testing
  • Release validation

Staging uses separate infrastructure and credentials.

docs.title: Production Environment
docs.text:
Production provides:

  • HTTPS
  • Automatic backups
  • Monitoring
  • Logging
  • Alerting
  • High availability
  • Independent scaling

Critical services should run on dedicated infrastructure.

docs.title: Scalability
docs.text:
The following components can scale independently:

  • Backend
  • Worker
  • Admin Web
  • PostgreSQL (future read replicas)
  • Redis

Future enhancements may include:

  • Kubernetes
  • API Gateway
  • CDN
  • Database partitioning

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text:
Production monitoring includes:

  • API health
  • Worker health
  • Database health
  • Redis health
  • Queue depth
  • Error rates
  • Response times

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
Application logs include:

  • API requests
  • Authentication events
  • Background jobs
  • System errors

Sensitive information shall never be logged.

docs.title: Backup Strategy
docs.text:
PostgreSQL:

  • Daily backups
  • Point-in-time recovery

Redis:

  • Persistence enabled
  • Recoverable from PostgreSQL where applicable

Object Storage:

  • Versioning
  • Replication
  • Backup verification

docs.title: Disaster Recovery
docs.text:
Recovery procedures shall include:

  • Database restoration
  • Object storage recovery
  • Redis rebuild
  • Worker restart
  • Backend redeployment

Recovery procedures should be periodically tested.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Production deployment shall provide:

  • HTTPS
  • TLS encryption
  • Firewall protection
  • Private database network
  • Private Redis instance
  • Restricted object storage
  • Secret management
  • Network isolation

docs.title: Configuration Management
docs.text:
Environment-specific configuration shall be externalized.

Examples include:

  • Database connection
  • Redis connection
  • JWT secrets
  • FCM credentials
  • SMS provider credentials
  • Object storage configuration

Configuration shall never be hardcoded.

docs.title: Future Evolution
docs.text:
Future versions may introduce:

  • Kubernetes
  • API Gateway
  • CDN
  • Service Mesh
  • Read replicas
  • Multi-region deployment

The deployment architecture supports gradual evolution without redesigning the application.

docs.title: Out of Scope
docs.text:
This document does not define:

  • CI/CD pipelines
  • Infrastructure-as-Code
  • Dockerfiles
  • Kubernetes manifests
  • Cloud provider configuration

These belong to implementation and DevOps documentation.
